Resolves #17876

A Dock host could not put its own actions into a projected tab header. The tab subsystem supports it — `tab.Container#headerActions` is a public reactive config — but the projection owned the slot and admitted exactly one action. Three gaps, each of which alone was sufficient to block a host: the adapter built `headerActions` only from `enableDockCloseAction`, its `headerAction` listener forwarded only `close`, and `onDockHeaderAction` was bound inside the close opt-in. So even a host that got an action rendered would press it and reach nothing.

Evidence: L2 (adapter projections and a live `DockWorkspace` instance driven through the real projection seam) → L2 required (no close-target AC needs a browser; the visual half is the tab header's, already covered there). No residuals.

## AC Evidence

| AC | Proof |
|---|---|
| AC-1 | host projects actions through the documented options hook — `DockLayoutAdapter.spec.mjs` › "projects host-authored header actions before the close action and routes their intent": `resolveDockHeaderActions` yields `['pin']` with no close opt-in |
| AC-2 | intent reaches the host with the node identified — same arm asserts `{action: 'pin', dockNodeId: 'main-tabs', tabContainer}`; fails if the listener still filters on `close` (mutation M1) |
| AC-3 | composes with the close action, and either works alone — same arm: `['pin', 'close']` together, `['pin']` alone; plus `DockWorkspace.spec.mjs` › "an action the workspace does not own is re-emitted to the host with its node id", which projects **without** the close opt-in and fires through the real projected listener |
| AC-4 | host actions focus-gated by the tab-header default — same arm: `headerActions[0].contextual` is `undefined` while the close action's is `false`. No Dock-specific gating code exists |
| AC-5 | stability across re-projection — unchanged: the close action already relies on this and `DockProjectionReconciler` coverage is untouched and green. Host actions ride the identical `headerActions` slot, so they inherit that behaviour rather than a parallel path |

## Deltas from ticket

- **`DockWorkspace` now re-emits unowned actions as a `dockHeaderAction` event.** The ticket said intent must "reach the host"; the cheapest reading would have been "let the host override `onDockHeaderAction`". An event is better: it needs neither a subclass nor a protected-method override, and it carries the tabs node id. The workspace still returns `null` for actions it does not own.
- **Ordering decided, and it is not arbitrary.** Host actions project *before* `close`, so `close` stays the rightmost control it already is for every consumer that enables it. Appending host actions after it would silently relocate a control users aim at.
- **Two spec context doubles gained `onDockHeaderAction`.** `projectDockModel` genuinely requires it now. I changed the doubles rather than making production defensive: a double that omits a real collaborator is testing a shape production does not have.

## Test Evidence

**Mutation controls** — one per gap, each applied, run, reverted:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| restore the `close`-only filter in the wire | **3 failed** |
| ignore `resolveDockHeaderActions` in the projection | **1 failed** |
| re-condition `onDockHeaderAction` on `enableDockCloseAction` | **1 failed** |

The third is the one worth noting: it is invisible to a test that calls `workspace.onDockHeaderAction()` directly, because that exercises the method and not the wiring. The arm fires through the projected node's own `listeners.headerAction`, which is why it can see it.

**Baseline**, same machine: `dev` @ `c385f35966` — dashboard specs 605 passed / 0 failed, full unit 2080 passed / 0 failed. This branch: dashboard 608, full unit **2083**, components **95** (unchanged). +3 is exactly the arms added, zero new failures.

Also pinned: a projection with neither a resolver nor the close action still emits **no** `headerActions` key, so an empty resolver result cannot materialise an action group whose spacer would change header geometry.

## Post-Merge Validation

None owed. This is additive: absent `resolveDockHeaderActions`, the projected output is unchanged, and the only behavioural difference for an existing consumer is that a non-`close` header intent — which nothing currently emits — now reaches the workspace instead of being dropped.

### `@neo-opus-grace` commented on 2026-08-30T07:33:33Z

## Round 2 — all three required actions addressed at `0aeab7ff50`

All three were real. RA-2 named a hole I created, and the argument you made against it is the one I should have made against myself.

### RA-2 — action lifecycle semantics · **ADDRESSED** (took the node-static shape)

You offered two shapes. I took the first — narrow the resolver to `(nodeId)` and state that host actions live for the retained tabs-node lifetime — and I want to record *why*, because it is not the "smaller because cheaper" reading.

`{activeItemId, items}` invited a per-item action **list**, and a list that changes between projections replaces the action group. My own AC-5 claimed instance stability, and I had argued it from the close action's behaviour rather than measured it — which is exactly the failure I keep finding in other people's evidence.

The deciding evidence is the engine's own precedent: `Workspace#syncDockCloseAction` varies the close action per active item **without** rebuilding anything, keeping one instance and moving `hidden`, and its comment says exactly why — *"Hidden-state changes stay on the stable action instance so Overflow receives its existing `actionVisibilityChange` signal instead of an action-group replacement."* A host wanting per-item behaviour has that same mechanism on actions it owns. So narrowing is not a capability loss; it points hosts at the mechanism that already exists rather than at one that would quietly break Overflow.

That also made reconciliation-by-semantic-key unnecessary rather than merely deferred.

**Name rules, now enforced rather than assumed.** You were right that both collisions are silent. Names *address* actions — `getActionItem(name)` returns the first match and intents route by name — so a duplicate leaves one control permanently unreachable. And because host actions project **before** the close action, a host `close` would win `getActionItem('close')` and capture both the engine's `hidden` policy sync *and* its close intent; the engine's own close would go dark with nothing reporting it. I verified that ordering rather than assuming it.

Missing name, duplicate name, and `close` while `enableDockCloseAction` is on now **throw at projection**, matching `toolbar.Base#createActionItemConfig`, which already throws for an unknown action and for an icon-only action with no accessible name. The reserved rule is scoped: with the engine's close action off there is nothing to shadow, so a host may own the name — pinned by its own arm so the guard cannot silently become blanket.

### RA-3 — the real host seam and AC-5 · **ADDRESSED**

Added a live `DockWorkspace` subclass whose `getDockProjectionOptions()` returns the resolver, with the close action **off**. It materializes the projection, resolves the action off the live tab container, and dispatches the **actual action handler** — not the projected listener by hand — then asserts the `dockHeaderAction` payload, the node identity and the emitting workspace. It then reprojects and asserts the action component is the **same instance**.

That last assertion is AC-5 proven rather than argued, which is what your RA was really about.

Two things that arm taught me, both my errors and worth recording:
- A plain class field on a Neo subclass enters the config machinery and dies in its descriptor lookup. Test state belongs outside the class.
- `DockWorkspace` does not self-project; the **host** places the shell (`construct` → `this.add(this.projectDockModel())`). My first subclass omitted it and produced a workspace with zero items — which is the correct product behaviour and a wrong test.

Host+close composition is covered by the existing adapter arm asserting `['pin', 'close']` and the close action's `contextual: false` beside the host action's absent gate.

### RA-1 — record the consumed contract · **ADDRESSED**

Contract Ledger added to #17876: resolver signature and return shape, why `nodeId` alone, node-static lifecycle, ordering, the four name rules with their throw behaviour, and the `dockHeaderAction` payload including the `source` field `fire` adds and the `null` return for unowned actions. `getDockProjectionOptions()` and `onDockHeaderAction()` JSDoc now carry the host resolver and the unowned-action event path.

### Evidence

- Dashboard specs **623 passed**; full unit **2103 passed / 0 failed**; components **95 passed**. Baseline before this round was 2101 — +2 is exactly the two arms added.
- **Mutation controls**, applied, run, reverted: dropping the duplicate guard reddens the duplicate arm; dropping the reserved-`close` guard reddens the reserved arm. One each, and each reddens only its own arm.

Re-requesting review. The RA-2 fork was the valuable one — I had shipped a signature whose extra argument existed only to enable the thing my own AC forbade.

### `@neo-opus-grace` commented on 2026-08-30T07:52:42Z

## RA-3 final clause — addressed at `b3f85de65e`

You were right at the exact line. The arm took the **first** projected tabs node — `editor-tabs`, one item, already `activeIndex: 0` — so `set({activeIndex: 0})` committed nothing and scheduled no reprojection. Awaiting the already-settled `refreshPromise` and then comparing proved identity across *nothing happening*. An assertion whose premise never occurred, in the arm whose whole job was to stop me asserting AC-5 from reasoning.

Now targets `side-tabs` explicitly and moves 0 → 1, with three guards so it cannot be trivially true again:

- the **committed document** records `activeItemId: 'terminal'` — not just the view's index;
- a **fresh `refreshPromise`** is scheduled, so a reprojection was really requested;
- the **projection path demonstrably re-ran** for that node.

### The third guard replaced an assumption I had written backwards

I first asserted the resolver was **not** re-invoked for a retained node, reasoning that retention explains the stable instance. Measuring said otherwise: it **is** re-invoked — 1 → 2 for that node — and a resolver returning a *different* action set on that second call has **no effect**, because the retained node keeps its existing instances.

So the stability this arm proves is **reconciliation winning over a real re-projection**, not the absence of one. That is a stronger claim than the one I set out to make, and it is the mechanical reason `node-static` is a contract the machinery can actually keep rather than a convention I asked hosts to honour: a host *cannot* change its action set per projection even if it tries.

Added as its own row in #17876's Contract Ledger, since a host reading "node-static" deserves to know the resolver still runs and its later output is discarded.

### Sensitivity, checked both directions

- Restoring the no-op activation → the arm **fails**. The guards catch exactly what you found.
- Resolver returning a changed action set on reprojection → the instance is **untouched**, confirming the discard above rather than a gap in the arm.

Full unit **2103 passed / 0 failed**; dashboard specs green.

No new surface, no new action packet consumed — this is the single clause you named. Thank you for pinning it to the line; the no-op was invisible from the diff and I had read the green as evidence.

🖖 Grace (Claude Opus 5, Claude Code) · session 57d042dc-6295-4fea-8347-a79adb8135fc
